tracks.title: Deployed software you can't diff
tracks.text: Lesson 02 point 8 — gitops. A sub-lesson, under the nexus. Start with the problem. Deployed software you can't diff. An agent is editing your live system… while it runs. Adding a post. Reshaping a page. And three questions follow immediately. First… what changed? Second… can you trust that record? And third… how do you push your own change into the running system, without stepping on the agent — and without standing up a deploy pipeline for every edit? [curious] The classic answers fail in opposite directions. Redeploying flattens the agent's in-flight work — the tar-over-ssh that copies a fresh tree over the box erases whatever the agent wrote since the last build. That clobber is the origin story for this whole subsystem. And the other answer — the agent says it updated the page — is not an audit trail. So the requirement is sharp. Every change has a diff. The record is the kind a stranger can check. And edits flow in and out, without either side erasing the other. There's a forty-year-old tool shaped exactly like that.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. gitops is the discipline where the engine's per-tenant data root… is a git repo. Agent commits flow out as the public changelog. Your pushes flow in as live updates. And access to the repo is the authorization — no deploy pipeline in between. It is not… we integrate with git. The runtime's files — org sources, page content, built output — literally live in a repo, one per tenant. So history, diff, and rollback are free. And the loop has exactly two directions. Outbound — the agent commits, the host publishes the site, then pushes to origin, all in one step. And inbound — a human or CI push is fetched and merged in on the keeper tick, live within one tick. The repo is the versioned source of truth. A small SQLite index rides alongside it for speed. And the git layer is a thin wrapper that shells to the git command line — the same discipline by which the package manager shells to cargo and bun.

tracks.title: Every deploy is a commit
tracks.text: Every deploy is a commit. Deploying a workbook does two things in one call. It writes the SQLite index… and it commits to the tenant repo. The commit message is, deploy, then the name. And here's the part that earns its keep — the commit's author is the authenticated identity. Git's attribution becomes auth's who. Picture the sequence. An authenticated client asks the control plane to deploy a workbook called lander. The plane updates the index — the fast lookup — and in the same operation writes a git commit… deploy lander… authored as the tenant identity. Two records, one act. A queryable index for speed… and a content-addressed commit for history. So the question, who shipped this, already has a hard answer — you don't bolt an audit log on later. [sighs] One scar lives here. Every git operation runs with a safe-directory flag, because on a deployed box a uid mismatch made git silently refuse every command. Agents wrote stories to disk for days… that never shipped, because the commit quietly failed. The lesson — a silent git is worse than a loud one.

tracks.title: Commits are the changelog
tracks.text: Commits are the changelog. The keeper — the agent on the tick — does its work inside the tenant repo. Its working directory is the repo. So the keeper's commits don't feed the changelog… they are the changelog. There's no separate release-note step that can drift from what actually happened. And that history is readable without an account. An anonymous request to slash underscore changes, on the public plane, returns the app's real git log — capped at thirty entries — plus the keeper's status. Picture three rows of it. First row — sha three-f-a-nine, author dev, message: deploy lander. Second — author dev, message: blog, ship growth post. Third — author dev, message: agent, refresh pricing copy. Four fields each — sha, timestamp, author, message — and that is the whole public record. A verifiable history… not marketing. [curious] The mechanics of the feed itself — the planes, the player — belong to the changelogs sibling lesson. Here it's enough to know — the feed is the literal log, and the log is the literal truth.

tracks.title: Commit, publish, push — atomically
tracks.text: Now the outbound half. Commit… publish… push — atomically. An agent does not run git. The git tool is host-brokered — the agent supplies only a commit message, and the host does the rest. An agent with no exec capability is told plainly… git not permitted. The agent never holds the keys to the repo. It asks the host to record a change. Walk the flow top to bottom. A tool call arrives carrying one string — the message, blog, ship growth post. The host first ensures the auto-written gitignore… so the bulk add that follows can sweep the whole tree without ever catching the signing key or the agent's scratch. It commits as the tenant. Then — and this is the load-bearing edge — it publishes content and blog to the served site root, in the same call, before it even tries to push. Finally it pushes, best-effort, and hands back the sha — three-f-a-nine, pushed, published four. [curious] Why weld publish to commit? Because the lander once shipped blog posts that were committed… but returned 404. The run died between the commit and a separate publish step. So the post existed in history… but never on the page. Fold publish into the commit, and the gap closes — if it's committed, it's served. The push is the only soft part. The returned sha carries its honesty as a suffix — pushed… or push failed… or committed, no origin remote to push.

tracks.title: Push to live
tracks.text: The inbound half — push to live. Outbound is the agent talking. Inbound is you talking back. Set the gitops flag to one… and the keeper's tick begins with a reconcile. It fetches origin and merges. It integrates upstream — it never overwrites. A push to your repo lands live within one tick. Trace the steps. You push from a laptop — maybe an edited design dot org, maybe a freshly built dist folder. On the next tick, with gitops enabled, the keeper first snapshots any pending agent work into a work-in-progress commit, so nothing in flight is at risk. It fetches… and merges. Then it republishes content, and if your push carried a built front-end, it ships that dist to the site root — clearing stale assets first, doing nothing when there's no dist. The site is current within that single tick. [curious] And the reconcile is best-effort by design — a failure is logged, and the run continues, never blocked.

tracks.title: Why merge, not overwrite
tracks.text: Why merge… not overwrite? This is the answer to the question everyone actually has — will this eat my agent's work? No. And the reason is a convention, not luck. The repo has two lanes that, in normal use, write disjoint paths. First lane — code. The app source, the agent definition, design dot org, the skills. Humans and CI write it, and you push it from a laptop or a pipeline. Second lane — data. Content, blog, the plan file, the dreaming folder. The agent writes it live, and the host pushes it on commit. Because the lanes don't touch the same files, a merge replays cleanly… and both survive. Your design dot org and the agent's content post land side by side. Only when the same file diverges does git stop — the reconcile returns a conflict, runs merge abort, and leaves it for a human. Never a silent overwrite. And this isn't asserted on faith — it's a test. Picture the timeline. On the laptop, a human clones, edits design dot org to canon v2, and pushes. Meanwhile the live agent writes content post v2, and the host commits it. On the next tick, the keeper logs… GitOps, pulled one upstream commit, one file, design dot org. And afterward both files are present — each at its author's version. [excited] Swap in a same-file edit, and the last line reads instead… GitOps conflict, design dot org, merge aborted, left for a human. The canon doc records the status as live-proven — an external GitHub push, pulled live.

tracks.title: What never enters the repo
tracks.text: What never enters the repo. A repo that an agent stages the whole tree against needs a bright line around what must never be committed. And there is exactly one such line — a module called Private, the single source of truth for session and personal data across every egress. Git… bundle… library, all of it. It exists because of a real leak — beads task data once pushed to GitHub. Now its ignore set is written into every tenant's gitignore automatically — which is precisely what makes the bulk stage safe. Run down what's excluded. First… the dot-workbooks folder — the per-tenant signing key, never in version control, by construction. Second… scratch, tmp, and memory — the agent's working space. Third… the beads and claude folders — task data and tool state, the leak that started all this. And fourth… the underscore sidecars — the steps log, the telemetry database, the ledger. The verdict — the agent's private life stays out of the public history by default. So the changelog is the work… and only the work. One module enforces it everywhere a byte could escape.

tracks.title: The repo carries a DID
tracks.text: The repo carries a DID. The signing key the ignore file protects is not decoration. Each tenant gets an Ed25519 keypair under the dot-workbooks folder… which becomes a real did-key — W3C and Radicle interoperable, the genuine article. And because a redeploy wipes the container filesystem, the primary tenant's keypair restores deterministically from a signing-key secret — so identity survives the box being rebuilt. Now follow the chain. Every step the agent takes appends a line to the steps log. The ledger seals those lines into a hash chain — each link is the sha-256 of the previous hash, joined with the raw line, from a fixed genesis. Then it signs the head with the tenant's did-key. And the anchor step commits the sealed ledger into the repo — so the head is witnessed by git's own content-addressing. Tamper with a step… and the chain breaks, and the history shows it. [curious] A second native record corroborates this — a tool called jaylay colocates over the same repo purely for its operation log, and does nothing when it isn't present. The ledger lesson takes this all the way down.

tracks.title: Any forge, or none
tracks.text: Any forge… or none. Your tenant is plain git, so it can be mirrored anywhere. The wbx command line exposes this as two verbs — both calling the engine rather than your local git binary. The dependency audit even flags a local git as convertible — git exists engine-side, so call through the engine. Three forms, three outcomes. First… mirror, then a git URL — a plain push to any remote, host-agnostic. Second… mirror, then a bare word like github — that's a forge, so the gh tool auto-provisions a repo named wb-tenant, private by default, and pushes. And third… federate — that's Radicle, which mints a rad identifier for peer-to-peer. The forge lane picks whichever CLI is on PATH — gh for GitHub, glab for GitLab, tea for Gitea, in that priority. No CLI on PATH… no magic — you're told to create the remote yourself and mirror by URL. And Radicle is honest about its ceiling — rad keys are per-device, and using the tenant keypair as a delegate needs a feature that doesn't exist yet. The limitation is documented… not papered over.

tracks.title: Where it bites
tracks.text: Where it bites — the honesty section. gitops is real and live-proven… but it is not finished. And pretending otherwise would betray the whole point of a verifiable changelog. First… the inbound flow is opt-in and keeper-coupled. Reconcile only runs when the gitops flag is set, and only on a keeper tick. No keeper… no push to live. A dedicated reconcile controller, with its own endpoint, is roadmap — not shipped. Second, the honest gap — the build seam. The runtime can't run a vite build — there's no bun on the BEAM box. So app-source pushes ride a CI bridge — a workflow builds, commits the dist back with a skip-ci marker, and the runtime pulls source and serves the built output. Push source, get a live page, no redeploy — but a CI hop in the middle. Retiring it means building in the sandbox on pull… and that's blocked on a concrete wall. QuickJS has no JIT, and re-parses the multi-megabyte svelte compiler every build — roughly seventeen CPU-minutes. The fixes are mapped — bytecode precompile, a warm instance, a cache — but not done. And the soft edges. A same-file conflict halts and waits for a human, rather than guessing. Forge provisioning needs a CLI on PATH. And the Radicle delegate limitation is upstream, not ours to fix. [sighs] None of these is hidden in the code… and none should be hidden from you.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Can I clone my tenant repo? Yes — it's plain git. Mirror it to any remote you control, or let a forge CLI provision one, then clone it like any other repo. No proprietary format underneath. Will a push overwrite what the agent is doing? No. Inbound is a merge, never an overwrite. Code paths and data paths are disjoint, so both sides survive — only a same-file divergence stops, and that one aborts and waits. A checked-in test proves it. Why isn't my push live? Three usual causes. The gitops flag is unset. Or there's no keeper ticking. Or the tenant has no origin remote. Check those in that order. Does my agent's memory get pushed? No — the auto-gitignore keeps scratch, memory, keys, and telemetry out by default. The changelog is the work, not the agent's private life. Is this how the platform itself releases? No — that's CI, a separate concern. gitops is tenant-level — it's how your running system records and accepts changes. And — what authorizes a push to take effect? Access to the repo. There's no separate deploy credential. If you can push to the tenant's origin… the next reconcile integrates it.

tracks.title: Back up to the nexus
tracks.text: So that's gitops. Your tenant is a repo — and that one fact carries everything. Commits flow out as the changelog. Pushes flow in by merge, never overwrite. And access to the repo is the authorization. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under the nexus — lesson two — where dev is prod, and you own the system you run. Beside it sit two more — changelogs, for the feed this page leaned on… and keepers, for the tick that hosts the reconcile. Everything gitops does… turns on that one idea. Your live system is a git repo.
